title: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Some families, many sub-families, very many genera and still more sections of genera are confined to a single region, and the most natural genera (those whose species are most closely related) are generally confined to one area.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Some few families, many sub-families, very many genera, and a still greater number of sections of genera are confined to a single region; and it has been observed by several naturalists, that the most natural genera, or those genera in which the species are most closely related to each other, are generally local, or confined to one area.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Centres of creation”. Scope: higher taxa (families, genera, sections) of plants and animals

fields.label: Assessment

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Global taxonomic occurrence data permit direct rank-specific range calculations. The secondary claim about naturalness needs interpretation but is still testable using phylogenetic cohesion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Calculate geographic occupancy and regional endemism for families, subfamilies, genera, and infrageneric groups, then relate genus range to within-genus phylogenetic cohesion. Support requires many lower higher-taxa to be single-region and cohesive genera to be especially local.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Endemism by taxonomic rank is directly countable from open catalogues and occurrences. Phylogenetic tightness of genera is available for a large share of plants and vertebrates, which is enough to test the correlation with range. Sampling bias toward widespread taxa is a known confound and can be reduced by using well-studied classes only.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compute the share of families and genera confined to one biogeographic region, and test whether genera whose species are phylogenetically closest have smaller ranges than genera whose species are loosely related. Widespread tightly knit genera as the rule would refute the second clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Wide-ranging genera are easier to name and sample, which can bias the range-relatedness correlation.

Most natural has to be translated into monophyly and short internal branches.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Across well-recorded classes of animals and plants, most genera (and a larger share of genera than of families) have essentially all of their modern occurrence records within a single continental region; and among mammal genera, those whose species are most closely related (youngest crown age in a dated phylogeny) occupy fewer regions and are more often confined to a single region than genera whose species are more distantly related.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: For seven GBIF backbone classes and each of seven GBIF continents, one faceted occurrence search (coordinates present, no geospatial issue, fossil and living specimens excluded) returned record counts per genus, family (and species for the smaller classes). Europe and Asia were merged into Eurasia. Taxa with >= 20 records were scored as confined if >= 95% of records fell in one region, and the fraction of confined taxa was compared between genera and families within each class. For mammals, genus crown ages were computed as the MRCA age of sampled congeners in the Upham et al. 2019 DNA-only MCC tree, genus names were matched to GBIF genus keys, and crown age was correlated (Spearman, and partial Spearman controlling log sampled richness) with the number of regions holding >= 5% of the genus's records; single-region fractions were compared between youngest and oldest crown-age terciles.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Clause 1 (regional confinement by rank): in each of the analysed classes (Mammalia, Aves, Amphibia, Reptilia, Magnoliopsida, Liliopsida, Pinopsida; GBIF backbone), the fraction of assessable genera that are confined to one region (>= 95% of their continent-assigned, non-fossil, non-captive occurrence records in one of six regions: Africa, Eurasia, North America, South America, Oceania, Antarctica) is > 0.50 in at least five of the seven classes, and in at least five of seven classes the confined fraction for genera exceeds the confined fraction for families. Clause 2 (natural genera are local, mammals): the Spearman partial correlation between genus crown age (MRCA age of the sampled congeneric species in the Upham et al. 2019 DNA-only MCC tree) and the number of regions holding >= 5% of the genus's records, controlling for log(number of sampled species in the genus), is positive with p < 0.05, AND the single-region fraction among genera in the youngest crown-age tercile exceeds that in the oldest tercile. The claim is 'supports' if both clauses pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if both fail.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Clause 1 fails if the confined fraction of genera is <= 0.50 in three or more of the seven classes, or genera are not more confined than families in three or more classes. Clause 2 fails if the partial Spearman correlation between crown age and number of regions is <= 0 or not significant at p < 0.05, or the youngest-tercile single-region fraction does not exceed the oldest-tercile fraction. Both clauses failing refutes the claim.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: mean across classes of the fraction of assessable genera with >= 95% of records in one region

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'region' is read as a continental biogeographic region (six regions, with Europe and Asia merged into Eurasia following Sclater's Palaearctic). 'Confined to a single region' is read with a 5% tolerance for misidentified, vagrant, introduced or mislabelled records. Sub-families and sections of genera are not available in the GBIF backbone and are not tested; the rank gradient is tested only between family and genus, with species reported as an extra. 'Most natural genera (species most closely related)' is read, following the assessors, as genera with the youngest crown age in a dated molecular phylogeny; this is a modern phylogenetic reinterpretation of a pre-evolutionary taxonomic notion. Only genera with >= 20 qualifying occurrence records are assessed, so that poorly recorded taxa do not appear confined merely through lack of records.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
GBIF occurrence search API, faceted counts by genus/family/species key per continent

GBIF Backbone Taxonomy species API (genus names for mammal genus keys)

Upham, Esselstyn & Jetz (2019) mammal phylogeny, DNA-only 4098-species node-dated MCC tree (NDexp, topoFree)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
GBIF 'Reptilia' (classKey 358) is a pro-parte synonym with no occurrences in the current backbone, so the pre-registered reptile class was run as Squamata (classKey 11592253), which holds most reptile genera.

GBIF continents are a coarse proxy for Darwin's biogeographic regions; merging Europe and Asia follows the Palaearctic but leaves Wallace's line and the Nearctic/Neotropical boundary at the continental edge.

Genus-level 'assessable' counts include extinct genera that have non-fossil basis-of-record entries and genera whose records are introductions or captives not flagged as LIVING_SPECIMEN; both bias against confinement, so clause 1 is conservative.

Recording effort is very uneven (Europe and North America dominate); the >= 20 record floor reduces but does not remove under-recording of tropical taxa, which could make some truly widespread genera look confined.

Clause 2 is a modern reinterpretation: 'most natural genera' was read as young crown age in a dated molecular tree. Crown age depends on which species were sampled (DNA-only tree) and on taxonomic lumping/splitting, and only 577 of 1890 assessable mammal genera had >= 2 sampled species. The negative partial correlation (older genera occupy fewer regions, controlling for richness) is significant but small.

Sub-families and sections of genera, which Darwin names explicitly, are not represented in the GBIF backbone and were not tested; the family-to-genus-to-species gradient is consistent with his rank ordering.
